newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Telstra payout pushes Canberra to headline surplus.
newsitem.headline: Telstra payout pushes Canberra to headline surplus.

text.p: Telstra Corp's special dividend of A$3 billion will push the Australian government's 1996/97 budget into a headline surplus on current fiscal figuring but will not affect the underlying budget balance.
A government official confirmed that latest published budget estimates, projecting a A$2.720 billion headline deficit, did not include the special dividend.
If government finances have not changed since those mid-year review estimates were published in January, the special dividend pushes the budget into a small headline surplus.

But the underlying budget -- currently forecast at A$8.5 billion -- excludes such equity transactions as the special dividend, counting them as "net advances", the difference between headline and underlying data.

Net advances are either inter-government loan transactions or equity transactions. Just as an equity injection into a government business is taken out of headline spending to leave the underlying account unchanged, a special dividend and its rundown of equity would be similarly be adjusted out.
Another government official confirmed that the Telstra payment would be treated in that fashion.
Budget statistics issued since the mid-year review suggest that the government's finances are broadly on track to meet the latest forecasts.
The current trajectory of revenue and expenditure is taking the government towards an underlying deficit in the region of A$8.5 billion to A$9 billion.
The data is always volatile, however, and analysts can only ever see an imprecise picture of what is happening.
The government did not budget for any significant rise in dividend receipts this fiscal year.
The budget and mid-year review both forecast A$4.0 billion in dividends, up only about A$100 million from the previous year.
Traditionally, most government dividends come from Telstra and the Reserve Bank of Australia.
According to the government's latest estimates, 1996/97 was to be the last year in which the government would return a headline deficit.
Even without special dividends and the like, headline surpluses are supposed to appear from next year.
The government cut its annual budget deficit by A$7 billion in full-year underlying terms last year and says it will cut again this year to eliminate the underlying deficit by 1998/99.
Since the mid-year review projected a deficit of about A$2 billion in 1998/99, cuts of at least that magnitude are expected in the budget to be announced on May 13.
Treasurer Peter Costello has expressly rejected the possibility of achieving an underlying balance in 1997/98, for which the mid-year review projects a deficit of about A$4 billion.
